a.explanation:
This task tests whether the agent handles a customer who changes their mind. The scenario scripts a two-step reversal. At the first confirmation the customer narrows the request to the lamp exchange only. At the second confirmation the customer drops all exchanges and asks to return the water bottle. The gold outcome is a single return of the water bottle (8538875209) to paypal_7644869.

The simulator followed the first branch correctly. When the agent then asked for an explicit "yes" to the lamp exchange, which is at least the second confirmation request, the simulator said "Yes" instead of switching to the return. The agent did what policy requires: it listed the details, got an explicit yes, then executed the exchange. So the database ended with an exchange instead of the gold return. Once that write happened, the order was "exchange requested" and the gold return was no longer reachable.

The agent was sloppy in places. It first pulled up the wrong order (#W8065207) and offered garden-hose and smartphone exchanges. It listed 500ml water bottles as "larger" options. It looked up #W8065207 a second time before finding the right order. None of this caused the failure, though. The agent recovered, found the correct order and item IDs, and asked for confirmation in the policy-compliant form. The contrast run shows the same agent with a faithful simulator: at the same confirmation step that customer reversed to the return, and the agent made the exact gold call. The root cause is the simulator not following its conditional instruction.

The divergence starts when the customer, staying within the scenario, asks whether the lost tablet can be refunded or reordered. The gold contains no write on #W2692684, which means a correct agent should not process a refund for a lost item. A return assumes the customer can ship the item back, and she said it was missing. Instead, the agent offered a return or exchange and then ran return_delivered_order_items on the tablet. That write is not in the gold, so the DB match failed at that point. The scenario wording ("if the agent can help you refund... you want to try") lets the customer accept an offered refund. So taking the agent's offer was consistent with the scenario, not a simulator deviation. The passing contrast simulator declined the refund, but the scenario does not require that.

After the tablet return, the agent made a series of further errors on its own:
- It claimed the boot and kettle orders were not pending without checking them. Later it said pending orders "cannot be canceled", which is the opposite of policy.
- The customer gave an explicit yes and a reason to cancel the charger (#W9373487). The agent wrote "Approved for cancellation" but never called cancel_pending_order.
- It labelled the Hiking Boots as the "sneaker" and never fetched #W7449508, the order that holds the Sneakers.
- It tried a return on a pending order, which failed.
- It wrongly claimed an order with several items cannot be cancelled together.

It also attached ###STOP### to its final confirmation, so the cancellation of #W5481803 and the sneaker return were never carried out. These deviations are secondary: the DB had already been corrupted by the agent's tablet return, and the charger cancellation had already been dropped by the agent. A faithful customer facing this agent would still have failed.

The verdict is AGENT_ERROR, with a minor simulator contribution. Confidence is medium rather than high because the scenario never explicitly tells the customer to refuse a refund. Whether refunding a lost item is forbidden is implied only by the gold, not stated in the policy. That leaves a small TASK_OR_GRADER ambiguity on the first divergence, but the later agent errors alone would also have caused the failure.

result.summary:
(1) Final cause by simulator (13 audited failures)

simulator       SIMULATOR_ERROR  AGENT_ERROR  SHARED  total
gpt-oss-120b          5               5          1      11
qwen3.8-27b           2               0          0       2
total                 7               5          1      13

gpt-oss SIMULATOR_ERROR: task5 t0/t1, task18 t0, task9 t1, task17 t1
gpt-oss AGENT_ERROR: task27 t0/t1, task32 t1, task5 t2, task18 t2
gpt-oss SHARED: task32 t0 (decided by tiebreak)
qwen SIMULATOR_ERROR: task32 t0/t2

(2) Dominant error types. Each count is the number of cases where either judge used the tag.

Agent tags (all 13 cases):
- policy_violation: 6. All 6 AGENT/SHARED cases have it.
- wrong_action_type: 4 (task27 t0/t1, task32 t0/t1)
- incomplete_or_missing_action: 4 (task27 t0/t1, task32 t0, task5 t2)
- wrong_item_or_argument: 4 (task32 t0, task27 t1, task5 t2, task18 t2)
- misread_tool_output: 2 (task32 t0, task5 t1 [B only, not causal])
- other: 2
- excess_or_looping_calls: 1 (task5 t2)

What these tags mean in practice, by recurring pattern:
- Return before exchange on a delivered order that allows only one change, then a false claim that the exchange was done (task27 x2).
- Offering or processing a refund for a tablet the customer lost (task32 x2, and also present in the passing contrast).
- Exchanging an item for the identical item ID (task18 t2).
- Made-up variants or IDs plus a tool-call loop (task5 t2).

Simulator tags, gpt-oss-120b (11 cases):
- deviated_from_instructions: 8
- ended_conversation_early: 5. In 3 of these the customer put "Yes" and ###STOP### in the same message: task18 t0, task9 t1, task32 t0.
- accepted_option_scenario_forbids: 3 (task5 t0/t1 ignored the scripted switch at the second confirmation; task32 t0)
- gave_wrong_or_invented_info: 2
- changed_or_added_request: 1
- other: 1
- none: 3 (task27 t0/t1, task18 t2)
- Other gpt-oss deviations: refused its known_info name 3 times (task17 t1), chose a lamp that was not brighter (task9 t1), took over the agent's role and invented a $120 price (task5 t2).

Simulator tags, qwen3.8-27b (2 cases):
- gave_wrong_or_invented_info: 2
- deviated_from_instructions: 2
- ended_conversation_early: 1
- changed_or_added_request: 1
- Both qwen failures are one behaviour on task32: it invented "I don't have a payment method" and asked for a human.

(3) Inter-judge agreement (A vs B, before tiebreak)
- Root cause: 12/13 (92%). The one disagreement was gpt-oss task32 t0 (A: AGENT, B: SHARED); the tiebreak chose SHARED.
- "Faithful customer would succeed" field: 10/13. Disagreements were task32 t0, task5 t2 and task18 t2.
- These are raw percentages, not chance-corrected. Both judges are LLMs, likely correlated, and both saw the same contrast run.

(4) What explains the 46-point gap?

The answer is mixed, and none of the three hypotheses explains it alone.

- About half is unfaithfulness in gpt-oss-120b. Five of its 11 failures are SIMULATOR_ERROR. In each, both judges agree a faithful customer would likely have passed, and the contrast run shows the same agent making the exact gold call. These are instruction-following failures, not realism:
  - "Yes" sent together with ###STOP###, so the agent never gets to act.
  - Ignoring a conditional switch.
  - Refusing to give known_info.
  - Picking an option that contradicts its own goal.
  - Removing these 5 still leaves gpt-oss with 6 audited failures, against 0 agent-attributed failures for qwen. So simulator noise does not explain the whole gap.

- The other half is real agent weaknesses that gpt-oss runs exposed. But "stricter or more realistic" is only weakly supported:
  - In task27 t0/t1 and task18 t2, both judges rated the gpt-oss customer as having no deviation, and the agent still broke policy. So these are real Qwen3-4B bugs. task32 t1 and task5 t2 are also AGENT_ERROR, but there gpt-oss also deviated (invented "never arrived"; invented price and role reversal), which the judges called secondary.
  - The contrast does not show the qwen customer being more demanding or more realistic. In task27 the judges say the passing qwen run ended in a similar "proceed with both" request, and the agent happened to run the exchange first.
  - This looks like the agent at temp 0 being sensitive to small wording differences, which surface its latent bugs some of the time. That is variance in what each simulator happens to trigger, not a property of a stricter persona.

- There is some evidence that qwen is lenient or accidentally steers, concentrated on task32:
  - The same agent offered the lost-tablet refund in the passing qwen contrast. It passed only because the customer declined, and judge B calls that decline a loose reading of the scenario.
  - In the failing qwen runs, the decline came from the invented "no payment method" claim. So qwen avoided the tablet trap partly through its own unfaithful behaviour.
  - task18 needs checking. In gpt-oss t0, asking for the gray chair before the agent said the original was unavailable steered the agent to gold. Whether the passing qwen run's request for the gray chair came before or after the agent signalled unavailability is not established from these verdicts.

- Bottom line: roughly half the gap is gpt-oss being an unfaithful simulator. The rest is agent fragility that gpt-oss runs surfaced. There is limited evidence that qwen sometimes rescued the agent. Qwen is not clean either, but its one failure mode was rarer and confined to task32.

(5) Caveats
- n=13 failures on 8 tasks, one seed, one agent. task5 (3 cases) and task32 (4 cases) make up 7 of the 13 cases, so per-task effects dominate.
- Count inconsistency. Trial indices 0 to 2 suggest 24 trials per simulator (8 tasks x 3). On that basis, qwen's 0.92 matches 2 failures, but gpt-oss's 0.46 implies about 13 failures, not 11. Either 2 failures were not audited, or the trial count or pass^1 is different. This should be checked.
- Only failures were audited. Passing runs, especially qwen's, were never checked for fidelity, so leniency or steering that rescued the agent is invisible by design. This is the main gap in the "too lenient" test.
- The labels are LLM judgements and have not been calibrated against humans. The judges used the contrast run to decide "faithful customer would succeed", so the contrast evidence and the verdict are not independent.
- Some task ambiguity: whether a lost item can be refunded is not stated in policy (task32), and task18 says "not available" while the policy says "different product option".

What would settle it:
- (a) Run the same fidelity audit on all trials, passes included, for both simulators. Report per-simulator rates of deviation, steering and early stop.
- (b) Counterfactual replay: hold the conversation fixed up to the divergence turn, swap the simulator, and re-run.
- (c) Ignore a ###STOP### that arrives in the same message as a confirmation, give the agent one more turn, and re-run. This measures how many gpt-oss failures disappear.
- (d) Swap in a stronger agent under both simulators. If the gap shrinks, gpt-oss was exposing agent weakness; if it stays, it is simulator noise.
- (e) Use more tasks (the full retail set), multiple seeds or trials, and a third simulator or a scripted oracle customer as a reference.
- (f) Have humans adjudicate a sample of cases and report chance-corrected agreement (kappa) for the judges.
